extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic and philosophy; logicians and analytic philosophers
extracted.subtask_description: A close analytic framework for determining what a proposition means and what it asserts: whether it concerns names/ideas or real phenomena, and which class of matter‑of‑fact (existence, co‑existence, sequence, causation, resemblance) it asserts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on external phenomena, not ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary object of logical inquiry in a proposition is the relation between the two phenomena which the subject and predicate express, not the relation between the corresponding ideas or conceptions in the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat investigation of truth as 'contemplating and handling our ideas' or as studying things only 'at second hand' in the mind. When asserting 'fire causes heat' we mean the natural phenomenon fire causes the natural phenomenon heat, not that one idea causes another. Examples: digging is an operation on things themselves; believing has the facts themselves as its subject. Avoid analyses that reduce propositions to mere manipulations of ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition's immediate object is the matter of fact signified
rubrics_metrics.description: When asking what a proposition asserts, identify the 'matter of fact' to which assent is given; the truth of a proposition is the conformity of this matter of fact to reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: 'What is the immediate object of belief in this proposition?' and 'What is the thing expressed by the form called a Proposition, the conformity of which to fact constitutes truth?' This orients analysis away from verbal/formal considerations to the factual content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hobbes's name‑identity analysis applies only to proper names
rubrics_metrics.description: Hobbes's view that a proposition signifies the speaker's belief that the predicate is a name of the same thing as the subject is correct only for propositions where subject and predicate are proper names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the limitation: proper names are mere marks for individuals, so predicating one proper name of another only conveys identity (e.g., 'Hyde was Clarendon'). This account 'exhausts the meaning' of such predications but is inadequate for general or connotative names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze connotative names by connotation (attributes), not denotation
rubrics_metrics.description: For connotative (general or descriptive) terms, meaning resides in connotation—the set of attributes a term implies—rather than merely in the class of denoted individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When subject or predicate are connotative, focus on the attributes the terms connote. E.g., 'man' connotes a set of physical/mental attributes; 'mortal' connotes the attribute of eventual death. The truth of 'All men are mortal' depends on the constant accompaniment of the attributes, not on preexisting lists of individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: General propositions assert co‑existence or sequence of phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: A general affirmative proposition (like 'All men are mortal') asserts that the attributes connoted by the predicate constantly accompany those connoted by the subject — i.e., a co‑existence or a sequence between two phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret universal propositions as claims about attributes: they assert that whatever has the attributes of the subject will also have those of the predicate (co‑existence) or that one phenomenon follows another (sequence). This makes them empirical claims about regularities in phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five‑fold classification of matters‑of‑fact in propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: All non‑verbal propositions assert one of five kinds of matter‑of‑fact: Existence, Co‑existence, Sequence, Causation, or Resemblance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this exhaustive taxonomy to classify what a proposition is asserting. Example labels and meanings: Existence (simple being), Co‑existence (simultaneity or concurrence), Sequence (order in time), Causation (noumenon causing phenomena), Resemblance (likeness of sensations or attributes). The classification helps determine appropriate methods of inquiry and verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Order in Place and Co‑inherence of Attributes within Co‑existence
rubrics_metrics.description: Two distinct varieties of co‑existence are 'Order in Place' (spatial arrangement, numerical intervals) and 'Co‑inherence of Attributes' (concurrent attributes or functions within the same part/locality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the difference when analyzing propositions: 'Order in Place' applies to spatial arrangements; 'Co‑inherence' applies to combined properties or functions (e.g., properties of gold atoms, mental faculties). Treat co‑inherence as a complex case of co‑existence often involving potentialities rather than presently sensed phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid explaining classification by presupposing classes (ὕστερον προτέρον error)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not explain judgments or propositions by referring to classifications or general names that themselves presuppose the judgments; classification often follows from repeated judgments rather than precedes them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware circular explanations that suppose classes were predetermined and then used to justify propositions. For example, thinking of 'white objects' as a class comes after observing several white things, not before. Explanations must not reverse cause and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: General names gain definiteness by connoting attributes, not by fixed membership
rubrics_metrics.description: A general name has a definite meaning insofar as it names an indefinite variety of things possessing certain attributes; classes are not fixed lists of individuals but are characterized by attributes that can include newly discovered objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When new phenomena are observed that have the connoted attributes (e.g., combustible diamonds), they are included in the class. Hence truth of general propositions is not settled by reading a prior roll of members but by empirical examination of attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: When class membership is borderline, predicate may assert resemblance rather than possession
rubrics_metrics.description: In marginal cases where an object lacks clear possession of class‑defining properties but resembles the class more than others, predication often asserts resemblance and not full possession; expressions like 'is considered' or 'may be ranked' indicate this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful to distinguish between asserting that an object possesses the properties of a class and asserting that it resembles the class. In scientific/precise contexts, prefer qualified language when membership is debatable (e.g., 'this genus may be ranked as...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Assertions about substances (noumena) are grounded in phenomena and amount to causation claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions about substances or attributes (noumena) have meaning only in relation to the phenomena by which those noumena manifest; affirming the existence of a noumenon implies asserting causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze statements about 'Socrates' or 'substances' by reference to the series of phenomena they exhibit. Claims about the noumenon's existence or actions are really claims about causal relations among observable phenomena and should be treated accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class names for simple sensations connote mere resemblance
rubrics_metrics.description: Classifications that group simple sensations or feelings (e.g., sensations of white, feelings of tightness) are founded on unanalyzable resemblance rather than analyzable attributes; predicating such class names reports likeness to prior sensations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When predicates refer to sensations, interpret them as reports of resemblance to past experiences rather than as assertions of attribute conjunctions. This category is specifically distinct from other predicate types and resists further elemental analysis.
